chapter.name: Democracy
chapter.blurb: Meaning and roots of democracy, its constitutional principles and institutions, forms of democracy in the world, grassroots democracy and challenges.

scope_in.item: Meaning of democracy, Indian democratic traditions and the making of the Constitution
Popular sovereignty, universal adult franchise, rule of law and Fundamental Rights
Separation of powers, judiciary, accountability, multi-party system and the rights of vulnerable groups
Role of media, civil society, RTI and citizen participation
Direct, representative, parliamentary and presidential democracy with country examples
India's scale of democracy, the three tiers, grassroots democracy and women's participation
Challenges to democracy including misinformation and the Emergency of 1975-77

concepts.name: Meaning of democracy, its Indian roots and the Constitution
concepts.description: What democracy is, the democratic traditions of ancient India, and the making of the Constitution of India.
concepts.idea: Democracy is government in which power lies with citizens who elect representatives; India's democratic ethos has deep historical roots.
concepts.rule: Democracy rests on freedom, equality, justice, rights and duties. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The Constituent Assembly (formed 1946) took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. The Constitution can be amended under Article 368.
concepts.example: Vedic assemblies (sabha, samiti, vidatha), early republican ganas and the Bauddha Samghas show early collective decision-making.

questions.q: In a democracy the source of power and authority lies with
questions.a: the citizens

questions.q: Democracy is founded on the principles of
questions.a: freedom, equality, justice, rights and duties
o: freedom, equality, justice, rights and duties

questions.q: The Constitution of India came into force on 26 ____ 1950.
questions.a: January

questions.q: The Constitution of India was adopted on
questions.a: 26 November 1949

questions.q: India is called the world's largest democracy because of
questions.a: the scale of citizen participation, especially its number of voters
o: the scale of citizen participation, especially its number of voters

questions.q: The Bauddha Samghas show democratic traditions because their members
questions.a: could debate and choose their leader and decide by voting
o: could debate and choose their leader and decide by voting

questions.q: The Aikyamatya Sukta of the Rigveda stresses
questions.a: collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose
o: collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose

questions.q: The Constitution provides for amendments under Article 368 so that it
questions.a: remains flexible and responsive to changing needs
o: remains flexible and responsive to changing needs
is only a list of laws

questions.q: Why is the Constitution described as a dynamic document?
questions.a: The makers believed it should not be a rigid legal code but capable of evolving through its fundamental values, so it allows amendment under Article 368.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly was formed in
The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and ____ days to draft the Constitution.
The Constitution ensures that no citizen is discriminated against on the basis of
questions.a: religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
o: religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth

questions.q: Give two examples of democratic traditions in ancient India.
questions.a: The Vedic assemblies sabha, samiti and vidatha; the republican ganas or samghas; and the Bauddha Samghas that decided by discussion and voting.

questions.q: How did the freedom struggle and foreign influences help shape the Constitution?
questions.a: The long struggle against British rule revived and strengthened democratic ideas. The Constituent Assembly Debates were also influenced by the global spread of democratic values along with Indian traditions.

questions.q: Describe how the democratic ethos of India evolved from early times to the Constitution.
questions.a: Early assemblies and republics and the Samghas practised consultation; foreign rule limited participation; the freedom struggle revived democratic ideas; the Constituent Assembly of 1946 drafted the Constitution, adopted in 1949 and in force from 1950.
s: Effect of colonial rule and freedom struggle

questions.q: The Constitution guarantees and protects
questions.a: the Fundamental Rights of all citizens
o: the Fundamental Rights of all citizens
only the rights of the rich
only the rights of the government

questions.q: Why did democracy not emerge suddenly in India?
questions.a: It evolved through a long historical process from ancient assemblies and republics, through periods of foreign rule and the freedom struggle, to the Constitution.

questions.q: Explain the role of the Constitution in safeguarding the rights of the people in a democracy.
questions.a: It guarantees and protects Fundamental Rights, ensures equality without discrimination, sets up democratic institutions and processes for liberty, equality, justice and fraternity, and encourages participation at national, state and local levels.

questions.q: Ravi says India became democratic only after independence and had no earlier democratic ideas. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Consultation and collective decision-making appear in the Vedic assemblies, republican ganas and Bauddha Samghas, so democratic ideas have deep roots.

questions.q: A school cabinet votes on activities for Republic Day and the majority choice is taken. Explain which democratic values this shows.
questions.a: Discussion shows participation and respect for diverse opinions; voting shows equality of every member; accepting the majority decision shows accountability and fairness.

concepts.name: Principles of democracy: popular sovereignty, franchise, rule of law and rights
concepts.description: Popular sovereignty, universal adult franchise, the rule of law and the Fundamental Rights, Duties and Directive Principles.
concepts.idea: A democracy stands on certain non-negotiable principles guaranteed by the Constitution.
concepts.rule: Popular sovereignty: power lies with the people. Universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 and above may vote by secret ballot. Rule of law: no one is above the law. Six Fundamental Rights (Articles 14-32). Article 21A: right to education (2009).
concepts.example: The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) lets citizens approach courts to enforce their rights.

questions.q: Popular sovereignty means that
questions.a: the ultimate source of power lies with the people
o: the ultimate source of power lies with the people
power lies with the judges only

questions.q: The right of every citizen aged 18 and above to vote is called
questions.a: Universal Adult Franchise

questions.q: India's Constitution provides for ____ Fundamental Rights.
questions.a: six

questions.q: The Right to Constitutional Remedies is in
questions.a: Article 32

questions.q: The rule of law means that
questions.a: no one is above the law and everyone has equal protection of law
o: no one is above the law and everyone has equal protection of law

questions.q: Citizens vote by
questions.a: secret ballot

questions.q: Fundamental Rights are enforceable in
questions.a: courts of law

questions.q: Under the rule of law a citizen cannot be punished
questions.a: without following the procedure established by law
o: without following the procedure established by law

questions.q: Why is the rule of law important in a democracy?
questions.a: It ensures equality before the law, prevents misuse of power, protects rights, and promotes justice, accountability and trust in the democratic system.
s: Prevents misuse of power / promotes justice

questions.q: The Right to Equality covers Articles
The Right to Education, Article 21A, was added in ____.
Which right protects children from exploitation such as forced labour?
questions.a: Right Against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)

questions.q: Name the six Fundamental Rights.
questions.a: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right Against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.

questions.q: Under which Articles can citizens seek constitutional remedies for violation of rights?
questions.a: Articles 32 and 226 allow citizens to seek remedies for protection and reinforcement of their fundamental rights.

questions.q: Explain popular sovereignty and universal adult franchise and how they are linked.
questions.a: Popular sovereignty means the state derives its authority from the people. Universal adult franchise gives every citizen aged 18 and above the right to vote by secret ballot, so people exercise sovereignty by electing governments and representatives.

questions.q: Fundamental Rights are described as indivisible and inalienable, subject to
questions.a: reasonable restrictions in accordance with law
o: reasonable restrictions in accordance with law

questions.q: Why does the Constitution also outline Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles?
questions.a: Rights come with responsibilities of citizens, and the Directive Principles guide the State in making policies for the welfare of the people, so both support a healthy democracy.

questions.q: Explain how the principles of popular sovereignty, rule of law and Fundamental Rights protect citizens.
questions.a: Popular sovereignty keeps power with the people; the rule of law ensures nobody is above the law and stops arbitrary punishment; Fundamental Rights protect freedom and dignity and can be enforced by courts.

questions.q: Meera says voting is not necessary because the government is elected only once. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. People exercise popular sovereignty by voting regularly, which keeps the government accountable and gives all adults a voice.

questions.q: Give a short example of how the rule of law protects a citizen accused of a crime.
questions.a: The person cannot be punished without following the procedure established by law; they get a fair chance to defend themselves in court, which prevents arbitrary action.

concepts.name: Separation of powers, accountability and the multi-party system
concepts.description: The three organs of government, the independent judiciary, accountability and transparency, political parties and the protection of vulnerable groups.
concepts.idea: Power is divided among organs of government and checked so that no one abuses it.
concepts.rule: Legislature makes laws, executive implements them, judiciary interprets them. Accountability and transparency: RTI Act 2005, Question Hour, CAG, CIC, Lokpal, CVC. Multi-party system: the party or coalition with over 50 per cent of seats forms the government. Article 46 protects weaker sections.
concepts.example: The judiciary can review laws and amendments to ensure they agree with the Constitution.

questions.q: The legislature
questions.a: makes laws

questions.q: The executive
questions.a: implements laws

questions.q: The judiciary ____ the laws (interprets them).
questions.a: interprets

questions.q: The Right to Information Act was passed in
Separation of powers prevents
questions.a: concentration of power in any one organ
o: concentration of power in any one organ

questions.q: In a multi-party system, the party or coalition that gets more than 50 per cent of seats
questions.a: forms the government

questions.q: Question Hour in Parliament helps to
questions.a: check the government's work and hold it accountable
o: check the government's work and hold it accountable

questions.q: The judiciary can review a law that is inconsistent with the Constitution and
questions.a: declare it invalid

questions.q: What would happen if the same organ made, implemented and enforced laws?
questions.a: Power would be concentrated in one organ, so there would be no checks and balances and a greater chance of misuse of power and arbitrary action.
s: No checks and balances or misuse

questions.q: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) helps to
questions.a: ensure access to justice for all
o: ensure access to justice for all

questions.q: The largest opposing group in the legislature is the ____.
questions.a: opposition

questions.q: Which body audits government accounts?
questions.a: the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)

questions.q: Name two institutions that ensure accountability and transparency.
questions.a: The Comptroller and Auditor General, Central Information Commission, Lokpal and Central Vigilance Commission.

questions.q: What does Article 46 of the Constitution say about weaker sections?
questions.a: The State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, particularly Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
s: Mentions SC and ST and protection from injustice

questions.q: Explain how the three organs of government check each other with examples.
questions.a: Parliament can amend the Constitution but the judiciary can review such amendments. The executive's enforcement power is regulated by laws made by Parliament and can be reviewed by courts. The judiciary can strike down a law inconsistent with the Constitution.
s: Executive regulated by law and courts

questions.q: Political parties in India function within the framework of
questions.a: the Representation of the People Act and other rules
o: the Representation of the People Act and other rules

questions.q: Why is a multi-party system important in a democracy?
questions.a: Many parties represent diverse voices and interests, give people the power to choose the most suitable, and reflect the diversity of society, with an opposition to check the government.

questions.q: Explain accountability and transparency in Indian democracy with three examples.
questions.a: Governments are accountable through elections, public debate and civil society. Parliamentary procedures such as Question Hour and audit of accounts check the government. The RTI Act 2005 lets citizens seek information from government agencies.

questions.q: Sam says the judiciary should be controlled by the government so it can help it. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The judiciary must be impartial and independent so it can protect citizens' rights, review laws and act as a check on other organs.

questions.q: Give a local example for each: legislature, executive and judiciary, and say what each does.
questions.a: Legislature: the State Assembly makes laws. Executive: the district administration implements them. Judiciary: the local court settles disputes under the law.

concepts.name: The media, civil society and citizen participation
concepts.description: The role of the media as the fourth pillar, civil society, the making of the RTI Act and how citizens participate in democracy.
concepts.idea: Democracy depends on informed citizens, a free media and civil society that bridge people and the State.
concepts.rule: The media informs people and is called the fourth pillar of democracy. Civil society means voluntary groups, NGOs and community associations. The RTI Act 2005 was shaped through debate in Parliament and consultations. Programmes like NSS and NCC build civic responsibility.
concepts.example: A young citizen stays informed through newspapers, news programmes and responsible use of the internet.

questions.q: The media is called the
questions.a: fourth pillar of democracy

questions.q: Civil society refers to
questions.a: voluntary groups, NGOs and community associations
o: voluntary groups, NGOs and community associations

questions.q: The Right to Information Act came into force in ____.
NSS and NCC are programmes that build
questions.a: civic responsibility, social awareness and respect for democratic ideals
o: civic responsibility, social awareness and respect for democratic ideals

questions.q: The media keeps people informed and serves as
questions.a: a voice of the masses

questions.q: The RTI Act empowers citizens to
questions.a: seek information from government departments

questions.q: Civil society and community institutions act as bridges between
questions.a: citizens and the State

questions.q: Access to accurate and authentic information is important in a democracy because it
questions.a: helps citizens form informed opinions and take part effectively
o: helps citizens form informed opinions and take part effectively

questions.q: How did the RTI Act come into being through democratic processes?
questions.a: Concerns about transparency raised by citizens, journalists, civil society and elected representatives were examined by parliamentary committees and expert groups, debated in Parliament and refined through consultation before it was passed in 2005.
s: Concerns raised by citizens and civil society
Debated and passed in Parliament in 2005

questions.q: Which is a way for a student to take part in democracy?
questions.a: staying informed and joining community service
o: staying informed and joining community service

questions.q: Public Interest Litigation is one way civil society helps make democracy more ____.
questions.a: inclusive

questions.q: Newspapers, news channels and social media contribute to democracy by
questions.a: raising public issues that lead to their resolution
o: raising public issues that lead to their resolution

questions.q: Give two ways a young citizen can take part in democracy.
questions.a: Read newspapers and use the internet responsibly to stay informed, join NSS or NCC, take part in community activities and school councils, and respect democratic values daily.

questions.q: Why are trade unions, cooperatives and community institutions called democratic in spirit?
questions.a: They follow democratic ways such as discussion, participation and decisions by members, extending democratic functioning into everyday social life.

questions.q: Explain the role of the media in a democracy and how irresponsible use of social media can weaken it.
questions.a: The media informs people, voices public issues and holds the powerful to account. But misinformation and fake news on social media can mislead people, confuse public opinion and even cause conflict, which weakens informed decision-making.

questions.q: Which citizen action weakens democratic values?
questions.a: spreading misinformation

questions.q: Why is the strength of democracy said to lie in its citizens?
questions.a: Without citizens' participation, awareness of rights and duties and honesty, no democratic process or institution can work effectively or give meaningful results.

questions.q: Explain how civil society, the media and elected representatives together made the RTI law effective.
questions.a: Civil society, journalists and citizens raised concerns; the media publicised them; parliamentary committees and expert groups examined them; elected representatives debated and added safeguards for national security and efficiency; the law then empowered citizens to seek information.
s: Concerns raised by civil society and media
Parliament and experts examined and debated

questions.q: Tara says the media has no role in democracy because only elected people matter. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. The media informs citizens, reflects public opinion and is called the fourth pillar, helping citizens hold governments accountable.
s: Describes the role of the media

questions.q: Plan a class activity on a local issue such as cleanliness that shows participation, discussion and responsibility.
questions.a: Hold a model Gram Sabha: identify the issue, let students discuss and propose solutions, vote on a plan and assign responsibilities.

concepts.name: Forms of democracy across the world
concepts.description: Direct and representative democracy, parliamentary and presidential systems, and examples such as India, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and the United States.
concepts.idea: Democracies share values but organise power in different ways.
concepts.rule: Representative democracy: people elect representatives. Parliamentary: the executive is part of and accountable to the legislature (India, Canada). Presidential: the executive is independent and the President is elected by the people (USA). Direct democracy: citizens directly take most decisions (Switzerland). Federalism divides power between the Union and states.
concepts.example: The United Kingdom is a parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarchy and an unwritten constitution.

questions.q: In a representative democracy
questions.a: people elect their representatives
o: people govern directly all the time

questions.q: India is an example of
questions.a: a parliamentary democracy

questions.q: The United States of America is an example of a ____ democracy.
questions.a: presidential

questions.q: A country given as an example of direct democracy is
questions.a: Switzerland

questions.q: In a parliamentary democracy the executive
questions.a: is part of the legislature and accountable to it
o: is part of the legislature and accountable to it
is elected directly by the people

questions.q: In a presidential democracy
questions.a: the executive is independent of the legislature and the President is elected by the people
o: the executive is independent of the legislature and the President is elected by the people
the executive is part of the legislature

questions.q: Direct democracy is difficult in large countries because
questions.a: citizens directly take part in most decisions
o: citizens directly take part in most decisions

questions.q: Which country has a constitutional monarchy and an unwritten constitution?
questions.a: the United Kingdom

questions.q: Explain how systems of democracy differ.
questions.a: They differ in how power is shared, who takes part in decisions, and whether checks and balances exist, for example direct participation versus elected representatives, or parliamentary versus presidential.
s: How power is shared or who participates

questions.q: In India the President is the Head of State and the Head of Government is
questions.a: the Prime Minister

questions.q: India and ____ are both parliamentary democracies (a North American country).
questions.a: Canada

questions.q: Federalism means
questions.a: power and responsibilities are shared between the Union and state governments
o: power and responsibilities are shared between the Union and state governments

questions.q: State two features of India's democracy from the comparison table.
questions.a: Multi-party democracy, written constitution, Fundamental Rights and Duties, and federalism.

questions.q: What is sovereignty?
questions.a: Sovereignty comes from a Latin word meaning supreme. It refers to the supreme, final and independent legal authority of a State over its territory and citizens.

questions.q: Compare parliamentary and presidential democracy with one example of each.
questions.a: Parliamentary: executive is part of the legislature and accountable to it; people elect the legislature but not the executive; example India or Canada. Presidential: executive is independent of the legislature and the President is elected by the people and accountable to them; example the USA.

questions.q: In the school council example, Team D, where only selected candidates contest and opposition is weak, is
questions.a: not truly democratic

questions.q: Which team in the school council example resembles direct democracy and why?
questions.a: Team A, because all students gather in one place, elect the president and vote directly on major decisions.

questions.q: Explain why democracy does not follow a single model even though it has common principles.
questions.a: Freedom, equality, participation, rule of law, rights and duties are common principles, but countries institutionalise democracy differently depending on how citizens participate and how power is structured, such as direct or representative, parliamentary or presidential, federal or unitary.

questions.q: Ali says a country is democratic just because it holds elections. Evaluate.
questions.a: Not always. Elections must be free and fair with open contest, multiple parties, freedom of expression and checks on power. Where only selected candidates contest and opposition is discouraged, democracy is weak.
s: Says elections alone are not enough
Names conditions such as free contest or opposition

questions.q: Choose two neighbouring countries and list four questions you would ask to decide whether they are democratic, partly democratic or non-democratic.
questions.a: Are regular elections held? Who chooses the Head of Government? Is there more than one political party? How free are citizens to express opinions and criticise the government?
s: Question about head of government or parties

concepts.name: India's living democracy and grassroots democracy
concepts.description: The scale of Indian democracy, the three-tier system, Autonomous District Councils and PESA, grassroots examples and women's voting rights and reservation.
concepts.idea: India's democracy is huge in scale and works at Union, State and local levels, giving villages a voice.
concepts.rule: India had over 96.8 crore voters in 2024, over a million polling stations, elections in 22 scheduled languages, over 2,800 registered parties. Three tiers: Union, State, Local. ADCs and PESA (1996) protect tribal areas. Article 243(d) gives one-third reservation for women in Panchayats; Article 243(t) in Municipalities.
concepts.example: Jethipura Gram Panchayat of Gujarat won the 2019 Gram Sabha award for people's participation.

questions.q: In 2024 India had over how many registered voters?
questions.a: 96.8 crore

questions.q: India's constitutional framework has three tiers:
questions.a: Union, State and Local governments

questions.q: Election symbols help voters who cannot ____.
questions.a: read

questions.q: PESA stands for
questions.a: Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas

questions.q: More than one million polling stations are set up
questions.a: even in remote areas like mountains, forests, deserts and islands
o: even in remote areas like mountains, forests, deserts and islands

questions.q: Elections in India are conducted in
questions.a: 22 scheduled languages and others

questions.q: The Autonomous District Councils in the north-east
questions.a: have legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs
o: have legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs

questions.q: The PESA Act empowers
questions.a: the Gram Sabha as the primary decision-making body in tribal areas
o: the Gram Sabha as the primary decision-making body in tribal areas

questions.q: Why is India called a "living" democracy?
questions.a: Its diverse electorate actively takes part in elections and local government, so democracy is sustained by continuous public involvement, not just by size.
s: Sustained involvement through elections and local bodies

questions.q: On average a Member of Parliament represents about
questions.a: 25 lakh people

questions.q: India has over ____ registered political parties.
Article 243(d) provides not less than what reservation for women in Panchayats?
questions.a: one-third

questions.q: How did women's voting rights in India differ from Britain and the USA?
questions.a: In Britain women got full voting rights in 1928 and in the USA in 1920 after long protests. In India Universal Adult Franchise was extended to women and men alike when the Constitution came into force in 1950, without prolonged struggle.
s: Britain and USA after long struggle

questions.q: Name two initiatives of the Jethipura Gram Panchayat.
questions.a: It ensured effective Gram Sabhas and record maintenance, organised Special Gram Sabhas and Mahila Sabhas, ensured a proper quorum with participation of marginalised groups, and acted on education, sanitation and welfare.

questions.q: Explain how the South Manubankul Gram Panchayat shows grassroots democracy.
questions.a: It is a "women-friendly panchayat" that promotes women's participation in decisions, offers facilities for health, sanitation and livelihoods, supports self-help groups and implements government schemes, showing an inclusive and responsive local government.

questions.q: The right to vote does not automatically ensure equal participation because
questions.a: social prejudices act as barriers to women's representation
o: social prejudices act as barriers to women's representation

questions.q: Why did some states go beyond one-third and give 50 per cent reservation for women?
questions.a: To increase women's representation and empowerment in decision-making, since social prejudices limit adequate participation despite the right to vote.

questions.q: Explain how local bodies show that democracy is more than voting.
questions.a: Citizens take part through Gram Sabhas, Mahila Sabhas, committees and local councils in planning, records, education, sanitation and welfare. This makes democracy responsive and inclusive at all levels beyond elections.

questions.q: Vik says only the Union government matters in a democracy. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. India has a three-tier system, and local bodies like Panchayats and Municipalities give citizens a direct say in local development.
s: Mentions three tiers or local bodies

questions.q: Suggest how your Gram Panchayat or Municipality could make women's participation stronger.
questions.a: Hold Mahila Sabhas, ensure reserved seats are filled, give women information and training, provide safe timings and facilities for meetings, and involve women in health and sanitation planning.
s: One measure such as Mahila Sabha

concepts.name: Challenges to democracy: misinformation, inequality and the Emergency
concepts.description: Challenges such as illiteracy, fake news and inequality, the Emergency of 1975-77 and the responsibilities of citizens.
concepts.idea: Democracy needs constant care; challenges are met by informed, active citizens and constitutional safeguards.
concepts.rule: Challenges: illiteracy, misinformation and fake news, inequality, poverty, regionalism, gender inequality, discrimination, gaps in implementing laws. The Emergency of 1975-77 suspended most Fundamental Rights, censored the press and arrested leaders; elections in 1977 showed the strength of democracy.
concepts.example: Damaging public property or spreading rumours weakens democratic values.

questions.q: A major concern in recent times for democracy is
questions.a: the spread of fake news through digital platforms
o: the spread of fake news through digital platforms

questions.q: The National Emergency was imposed in India in
The Emergency was lifted in ____.
Jayaprakash Narayan was popularly known as
questions.a: Lok Nayak

questions.q: During the Emergency
questions.a: most Fundamental Rights were suspended and the press was censored
o: most Fundamental Rights were suspended and the press was censored

questions.q: After the Emergency was lifted, general elections were held and
questions.a: the ruling government was defeated
o: the ruling government won by a large margin

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a challenge to democracy?
questions.a: illiteracy, misinformation and inequality

questions.q: Which action weakens democratic values?
questions.a: damaging public property or spreading misinformation
o: damaging public property or spreading misinformation

questions.q: What led to widespread protests before the Emergency?
questions.a: Rising unemployment, inflation and allegations of misgovernance under the government of the time caused public dissatisfaction and protests.

questions.q: Which social barrier is mentioned as creating obstacles to equal participation?
questions.a: gender inequality and social discrimination

questions.q: Programmes like NSS and ____ build civic responsibility.
questions.a: NCC

questions.q: The Emergency period showed both
questions.a: the vulnerabilities and the resilience of Indian democracy
o: the vulnerabilities and the resilience of Indian democracy
the end of democracy for ever
the weakness of the Constitution only

questions.q: Name two challenges to democracy in India mentioned in the chapter.
questions.a: Illiteracy, misinformation (fake news), inequality, poverty, regionalism, gender inequality, social discrimination and gaps in implementing laws.

questions.q: How did the people show the strength of democracy after the Emergency?
questions.a: Through the general elections held in 1977 they expressed their will through the ballot and defeated the ruling government, showing the importance of constitutional safeguards, civil liberties and citizen participation.
s: Defeat of the ruling government by the ballot

questions.q: Describe the Emergency of 1975-77 and its effects.
questions.a: In June 1975 a National Emergency was imposed on grounds of internal disturbance. Most Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and many leaders and activists were arrested. Democratic institutions were strained. Mass movements led by Jayaprakash Narayan mobilised citizens, and it was lifted in 1977.

questions.q: Why is being well-informed a vital responsibility of a young citizen?
questions.a: It helps form informed opinions and take part positively in democracy
o: It helps form informed opinions and take part positively in democracy
It is required only for adults

questions.q: How can fake news harm democracy?
questions.a: It can influence public opinion, create confusion, mislead voters and sometimes lead to conflict, so decisions are not based on facts.
s: Can lead to conflict or poor decisions

questions.q: Explain why democracy is called a continuous process needing citizen care.
questions.a: The Constitution guarantees rights but expects people to use them responsibly. Democracy is shown in everyday behaviour and civic responsibility, and it can be weakened by misinformation, indifference or violations of rules, so it needs constant awareness and participation.

questions.q: Ravi says the Emergency shows that democracy in India is weak. Evaluate.
questions.a: The Emergency showed vulnerabilities, but the return of elections in 1977 and the defeat of the government showed the resilience of democracy and importance of safeguards and active citizens.

questions.q: Choose one civic activity for this month and explain how it strengthens democracy.
questions.a: Volunteering for a clean-up drive strengthens participation and responsibility; verifying news before sharing it protects against misinformation.
